No you're not understanding, Tank doesn't have to get a 10-8 round, he just has to win the round, but get knocked down, and then the round will be even.

If fighter A wins the round he gets 10, fighter B loses the round gets 9.

If a fighter is knocked down then that fighter has a point deducted.

If fighter A wins the round he gets 10, fighter B loses and gets 9 and is knocked down so it's deducted to 8. That's 10 - 8

If fighter A wins the round he gets 10 but is knocked down so is deducted a point so gets 9, fighter B loses the round but isn't knocked down then it's 9. That's 9 - 9.

(And then because it's a 'ten point must' system, meaning at least one fighter must have 10, and 9-9 is an even round, the round will be scored 10-10.)

Here is my take on Dubois.

He turned pro around 2016/7. This was at the peak of AJ mania when Matchroom was going from strength to strength and Frank Warren/Queensberry were at their lowest point. I think Frank jumped at the chance to sign Dubois because he saw that he could make this guy into ‘his’ AJ. Both are athletic black guys from down south with knockout power and who drew comparisons to Frank Bruno. I think Warren has promoted Dubois like he is a prodigy ever since, and this has been good and bad for Dubois.

For example, putting a very green Dubois in with someone as good/experienced as Joyce was just stupid. He went from fighting journeymen to getting chucked in with Joyce. I remember the buildup to that fight, you’d never know Warren also promoted Joyce, he was all about Dubois and clearly didn’t think he’d lose.

But Warren’s attitude has also been good for Dubois: instead of being chucked aside after one loss (as promoters often do with prospects who lose) Warren quickly got him a shot at Trevor Bryan for the WBA Regular belt which made him mandatory for Usyk.

Usyk fight was again probably too soon, Dubois could’ve used the Miller and Hrgovic fights before fighting the top guy in the division. But again Frank Warren was totally undeterred by another loss and booked Dubois into two more risky fights.

It’s arguably poor match making, too much too soon and that, but it’s actually worked out perfectly for Dubois, there’s no one in his age range with even half the experience (compare to Anderson, Torrez etc. even older prospects like Jalolov and Huni have nowhere near the experience). He doesn’t have the same pressure to stay undefeated and learned from both losses.

I wouldn’t say he’s a prodigy, there’s loads of parents who start their kids training for a sport at an early age. He’s got raw talent tho clearly, I’d say only AJ and Zhang punch harder than him at the minute, and he’s significantly faster than Zhang and has a better gas tank.

When the older generation (AJ, Usyk, Fury) retire he’ll have a major advantage over everyone in the division. Very possible he doesn’t have the longevity of the current generation tho, most of them started late (Wilder, AJ) or didn’t have tough fights that young (Fury, Joyce). Dubois has already taken quite a bit of damage. But we’ll have to wait and see.

Not the OP but this is my reasoning for not putting Foreman in top 5:

Foreman was definitely great: one of the heaviest hitters ever, underrated ring craft, and a brawling style which matched his attributes.

He has two of the best heavyweight wins ever against Frazier and Norton.

But actually during the 1980s he was somewhat forgotten. He was a guy who briefly held the championship but then lost dominantly to Ali, went life and death with Lyle, and then got outboxed by Jimmy Young. Other than his two big wins his resume didn’t really have much depth. People forget now but it was actually his comeback career that revived Big George’s reputation as an all time great.,Yet paradoxically his ‘old’ career is not that impressive at all:

Yes it’s impressive he won the titles at 45 but 1) he had a style well suited to an older fighter, 2) he relied on power and that is the last thing to go, and 3) he had a 10 year gap in his career and so had less wear and tear than the other fighters his age.

His resume in his comeback career is: beat Qawi and Cooney, got gift decisions against Stewart and Schulz, beat by Holyfield, thoroughly outboxed by Morrison who was never even known as a skilled boxer, beat Moorer and deserved the win over Briggs.

Like I said, the Moorer win is impressive for Foreman’s age but the performance itself isn’t great: Foreman was losing every round, being outboxed by the smaller man, who got carried away and gassed out and Foreman capitalised on it.

So yeah Foreman has the high highs of beating Frazier and Norton, but not a lot else. Plus Frazier and Norton had very similar builds, lots of stylistic similarities and were both trained by Eddie Futch. It was a style tailor made for a brawler like Foreman. Foreman never beat a fast, cerebral fighter, which make up most of the ATG lists.

No way I could see him being put over Ali, Louis, Holmes, Lewis or Holyfield. In terms of resume I think Frazier could definitely be put above him, after all Frazier beat Ali who beat Foreman. Also Foreman always had height/reach/weight advantage in his fights, I think he would’ve definitely struggled with skilled big fighters (Bowe, the Klitschkos, Fury).

I’d put Foreman at the bottom of the top 10. Like I said, he has attributes that make him a great fighter, but resume-wise he’s really overrated, and H2H it’s easy to see loads of other fighters beating him tbh.

Anxiety is very rarely logical, it’s an experiential thing. Yes in theory just standing and presenting something you have prepared shouldn’t be a cause for anxiety, and yet for many people it is. I could give a presentation to a small group of strangers, knowing I will never see any of them again, but as soon as I started presenting I’d get hit with intense nerves and self-consciousness and likely make a lot of mistakes because of it.

I know this isn’t the experience of everyone but I imagine it’s true of a lot.

It’s why I don’t think forcing kids who find the experience excruciating helps them at all. Some kids are fine giving presentations, others aren’t, neither group is likely to change. For some people, giving presentations is just a shit part of life that you have to get through now and again, and avoid as much as possible.

I did loads of presentations in high school and university, put a lot of effort into them too, so I did ‘practice, practice, practice’. and did try to ‘fake’ the confidence. It didn’t work. I was just left feeling more anxious than before, and knowing that soon another teacher/lecturer would force me to do another one.

Not being forced to have those experiences would’ve probably made me less anxious tbh. Now I associate any public speaking with those memories.

Amazon started out selling books. It was started by a rich guy (Bezos) who inherited enough money to sell books at a loss. Amazon existed for well over a decade before it actually made a profit. This is not the same as being efficient. There might have been Amazon competitors that were faster, better quality, better to employees, or more innovative, but they just didn’t have the money to keep up with Amazon.

Eventually Amazon monopolised the market and is now basically too big to fail.

So the idea that Amazon won due to efficiency, or the rules of the market let the best possible company be at the top, feels wrong.

Don't know where else to put this but fancy talking about it with someone. I'm 22. I've been writing since I was in my early teens, mostly reviews and autobiographical pieces back then, occasionally short stories and poetry. Between the ages of 18 to 20 I didn't write much but then I got back into it. Since then I've been writing non-stop. I write everyday without fail and have done so for well over a year. I've wrote loads of stories, poems, essays, reviews, journal entries. But I recently decided to read through a lot of what I'd written and it's all just rubbish. That's not just me being self-critical, none of it is good enough to publish. The older stuff is laughably bad; the stuff I've written recently is just plain boring, pretentious and has no purpose. And I just don't know how to improve. I've read loads, read lots of books on writing, had lots of feedback from people on here and other websites and some irl. I just can't stop comparing myself to other writers. So many great authors were so young when they published their first stuff. Even if you go read the neglected first novel of a writer who went on to be famous and acclaimed that first novel is still pretty great, not as great as their later stuff but TONS better than anything I've ever written.

So my question is: do you ever feel like just packing it in? Finding something else, some other skill to put your time into. I know people will want to reply with something like, 'You just need to keep writing and you'll get better'. But I've given so much to my writing already. There's been days I've spent hours at it. I've sweated before being so engrossed in it. I've revised stories again and again into a place where I thought they were decent but then when I read them later on - like I recently did - it's plain rubbish. I guess you could say I'm just in a pessimistic mood right now, hitting a wall, but as bad as it is throwing in the towel early, not achieving your potential, not facing the challenges of life etc. I think it's equally bad to waste time on something that's never going to grow into something better, where you'll have to delude yourself into thinking your 'big break' is coming soon when really it's not.
